notes: Camp coverage is genuinely complete for the diagnostic fight as actually conducted. Two adjacent, currently-active schools are absent but non-blocking: (1) the deliberative/participatory renewal camp (Helene Landemore's Open Democracy, Van Reybrouck, DemocracyNext, the OECD 'deliberative wave'), which diagnoses populism as a symptom of electoral representation itself and prescribes sortition/citizens' assemblies — it is a remedy camp on a slightly different question, and its critique of technocratic closure is partially carried by the Corrective Populist position; (2) epistocracy/technocracy defenders (Jason Brennan, Garett Jones's '10% Less Democracy'), academically real but with little movement presence in this debate. Worth a line in a question detail or an action if the topic is ever expanded, not a parity failure now.

Actions tiering has a mild optical asymmetry: the two anti-populist camps' actions (V-Dem report, Protect Democracy) sit at tier 1 while the National Conservative, Corrective Populist, and Measurement Skeptic actions all sit at tier 2. Plausibly prevalence-driven for Erosion Diagnostician (weight 85), but Guardrail (40) at tier 1 vs National Conservative (45) at tier 2 is not explained by weight; consider swapping NatCon's Statement of Principles to tier 1 or Guardrail's donate to tier 2. Also only one camp gets a 'donate' and only one a 'volunteer'; kinds-per-camp asymmetry is minor but visible.

RepresentUs ranked-choice voting is a loose fit as the Corrective Populist action: RCV is a good-government/anti-duopoly reform, not a people-vs-oligarchy populist project, and Mouffe-style proponents would not recognize it as theirs. The technopopulism essay is the better on-voice action; consider replacing RepresentUs with something closer to the camp (e.g. a left-populist movement resource).

Measurement Skeptic's description/detail is written in a noticeably em-dash-heavy register while the other four positions use commas and parentheses for asides; harmless, but the style guide flags exactly this and a copyedit pass would even it out.

Levitsky & Way precision: the paper's 23-improved-vs-8-declined Freedom House comparison is framed as 1999-2013 (their 2000-2013 claim is about mean index scores across four indices); the draft says '23 vs 8 for 2000-2013'. One-year baseline slippage, not misleading, but easy to align with the source.

PopuList series mid-point: the draft's '~2016: 10%' vs the Sciences Po/PopuList communication's '11% in 2016'. Within rounding of the same dataset; if the chart is meant to quote the database's own communication, use 7% (2006) and 11% (2016).

Verification record for the editor — all load-bearing and post-cutoff claims checked against live sources today and confirmed: V-Dem 2026 (74% under autocracy, 1978 level, 44 autocratizing, 10 new incl. US/UK/Italy) via v-dem.net and democracywithoutborders.org; Freedom House 2026 (20th year, 54 vs 35, 21% Free) via freedomhouse.org; PopuList 23% via sciencespo.fr; TBI counts (4→19 peak 2019→12 early 2024) via institute.global; Hungary April 2026 Tisza landslide via CNN/Al Jazeera/Chatham House; Le Pen appeal 7 July 2026 (ineligibility cut to 45 months, 30 suspended, backdated, 2027 eligibility restored) via France24/Al Jazeera coverage; Cologne Administrative Court injunction on the AfD designation confirmed dated 26 Feb 2026 via France24; CEI 2,441 rules vs 133 laws (18-to-1) confirmed exactly via cei.org; Levitsky & Way 23-vs-8 via the Journal of Democracy text; OECD trust 39%/44% and Poland 74.4% turnout consistent with cited sources.

Optional why_now sharpener: Tisza won a two-thirds supermajority (141/199), the threshold to amend Hungary's Fundamental Law — a detail that strengthens the draft's own 'can backsliding be reversed' framing and could be added to the Basics deep tier at the next update.

Every camp reads as written by a believer. The National Conservative section is notably strong: it leads with the movement's own evidence (CEI rule counts, Le Pen/AfD asymmetry claim, Israel's judicial-selection framing) rather than a critic's paraphrase, and the internal Vermeule fault line is handled as proponents themselves debate it, not as a gotcha.

Measurement Skeptic proponents list includes Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way. Historically accurate (their 2015 'Myth of Democratic Recession' is a core text of that camp) and the detail dates it correctly, but both have since publicly argued backsliding is real, and Levitsky also anchors the opposing Erosion Diagnostician camp. Consider tagging them '(2015 argument)' in the proponents string so a reader doesn't take them as current skeptics.

Corrective Populist places the Western-Europe null result of the Leininger/Meijers turnout study inside the position's own description. A real Mouffe proponent would keep the CEE finding in the pitch and leave the null to the detail tier, where it is already handled well. Accuracy-preserving move would be to trim the 'though the same effect does not appear in Western Europe' clause from the description and let the detail carry it.

Measurement Skeptic steelman runs ~105 chars, slightly over the ~90-char banner target; the distribution stage can compress ('Count what autocrats do, not what experts feel: incumbents aren't winning more').

Erosion Diagnostician's steelman and description are proponent-voiced and strong; its detail even pre-empts the 'partisan complaint' charge with the Chavez/Orban symmetry point, which is exactly the argument Levitsky/Ziblatt themselves deploy.

blocking.issue: MISATTRIBUTED STAT (Guardrail Institutionalist description): "V-Dem's 2026 Democracy Report puts judicial and legislative constraints on executives at their lowest level in over a century, worsening in 21 countries against just 4 improving." I read the report text directly. The "lowest level in over 100 years" claim is US-specific, from Section 5 ("In Focus: Autocratization in the USA"): US Legislative Constraints fell from 0.86 to 0.61 in 2025, "the largest single-year drop in the US history, and 2025 is the lowest level in over 100 years"; US Judicial Constraints fell 0.90→0.84, "the lowest level since 1900." There is no global statement that executive constraints are at a century low. Separately, the 21-vs-4 count is global but covers Legislative Constraints ALONE over 2015–2025 ("Legislative Constraints on the executive are worsening in 21 countries and advancing in only four"); the parallel Rule of Law figure is 22 vs 7. The draft bundles judicial in with legislative and presents a US finding as a worldwide one.
blocking.fix: Rewrite as two separated, correctly scoped facts, e.g.: "V-Dem's 2026 Democracy Report finds legislative constraints on the executive worsening in 21 countries over the past decade against just four improving; in the US they lost a third of their value in 2025 alone, the lowest level in over 100 years."

blocking.issue: WRONG NUMBER vs the cited source (Basics, "Far-right vote share in Europe · 1995–2026"). The series point "~2016: 10%" contradicts The PopuList's own published reference figures, which are 7% (2006), 11% (2016) and 23% (2026); the "1995: 5%" point is not a figure the source publishes at all. The rounding also props up the note's claim of "more than double the share a decade earlier" — true against the real 11% but only barely (2.09x), so the draft states its own source slightly more strongly than the source supports.
blocking.fix: Use the source's published series: 2006 → 7%, 2016 → 11%, 2026 → 23% (drop or re-source the 1995 point), and keep the note as "more than double the share a decade earlier" — which still holds against 11%.

blocking.issue: UNSOURCED RESEARCH CLAIM stated as an established finding (Erosion Diagnostician, detail): "cross-national research on backsliding episodes finds the populist ideology of the executive is a stronger predictor than executive strength alone." No such head-to-head finding exists in the literature I could locate. The closest work — Ruth-Lovell, Lührmann & Grahn, "Democracy and Populism: Testing a Contentious Relationship" (V-Dem WP 91, 2019) — finds erosion of electoral, liberal and deliberative democracy under both left- and right-wing populist governments, but does not benchmark populist ideology against executive strength; the follow-up (Ruth-Lovell & Grahn 2023) finds the negative effect is MODERATED by prior strength of electoral democracy, which cuts toward the opposing camp. As written, the topic settles its own question 1 ("systematic pattern vs. institution-dependent") with a finding that isn't in evidence.
blocking.fix: Replace with the citable finding and drop the comparative claim: "…cross-national work by Ruth-Lovell, Lührmann and Grahn (V-Dem, 2019) finds electoral, liberal and deliberative democracy eroding under populist governments of both left and right, while the egalitarian and participatory gains populists promise do not appear." Keep the ideological-license argument as the camp's reading rather than as a research result.

notes: Verified accurate, no action needed: V-Dem 2026 (74% / ~6bn in autocracies, 7% / 0.6bn in liberal democracies, 1978 level, 44 autocratizing at 41% of population vs 18 democratizing at 5%, 179 countries splitting 31/56/57/35 — I counted Table 1 to confirm — and the 10 new autocratizers list exactly: Cambodia, Croatia, Italy, Kuwait, Madagascar, Slovakia, Slovenia, Togo, UK, USA, with five European plus the US = six in Europe/North America); Freedom House 2026 (20th year, 54 declining vs 35 improving, 46%→21% Free, coups/protest crackdowns/constitutional safeguards as drivers); OECD (39% vs 44%, 30 countries, ~60k respondents, late-2023 fieldwork, and the 18-country like-for-like 43→41 / 40→43 with Belgium and Colombia up, Finland and Norway down — precise and honestly caveated); PopuList v4.0 (23%, 30% anti-establishment, 31 countries, ~150 scholars, Rooduijn team); Poland turnout 74.38%, record since 1989; TSE 5–2, June 2023, ban to 2030; BfV 2 May 2025, suspended six days later, VG Köln 26 Feb 2026 injunction; Le Pen appeal 7 July 2026 (45 months, 30 suspended, backdated, eligible for 2027, declared within hours); CEI 2,441 rules vs 133 laws, 18-to-1; NatCon statement quote and June 2022 date; Leininger & Meijers (Political Studies 69(3), 2021, 315 elections, 31 democracies, CEE effect absent in Western Europe); Hungary's 12 April 2026 Tisza landslide. All 14 URLs resolve.

STALENESS (Poland deep stat, detail): "as of late 2024 all 15 Constitutional Tribunal judges remained PiS appointees" is dated and isolated, so it meets the durability rule, but it is 20 months old and there is a sharper 2026 fact: in March 2026 the Sejm elected six new judges, President Nawrocki swore in only two, the ECtHR issued an interim measure ordering the other four be seated, and the tribunal rejected it — while the Tusk government still refuses to publish its rulings. Updating to the 2026 standoff makes the same point more durably.

Question 5 detail: "Hungary's opposition has repeatedly won large vote shares without translating them into parliamentary seats under Fidesz-drawn electoral maps" is true of 2014/2018/2022 but now sits against the topic's own why_now (Tisza took 141 of 199 seats on ~53% in April 2026). Add "until 2026" or note that the maps eventually did not hold, so the pessimistic case is not silently overtaken by the news.

Measurement Skeptic detail: V-Dem's methodology states it typically gathers five experts per country-year observation (not "roughly 3–5"), and it does run cross-coder calibration via bridge coders and anchoring vignettes. "No ground-truth check" is fair as skeptic framing, but correct the coder count to "typically five" so the paragraph is not rebuttable on a checkable number.

Measurement Skeptic detail: the 23-improved vs 8-declined comparison in Levitsky & Way is for 1999–2013 (the four-index mean comparison is the 2000–2013 one). Adjust the date range attached to that specific pair.

Citation precision: Little & Meng appeared in PS: Political Science & Politics 57(2), April 2024 (online January 2024), and the reply's full title is "How Little and Meng's Objective Approach Fails in Democracies."

National Conservative description: CEI's own 2026 report notes that 2,441 final rules is an all-time low count; the 18-to-1 ratio is accurate as stated, but a half-clause acknowledging the falling rule count would keep the strongest version of the argument from being knocked over by its own source.
Two Basics stats (Poland turnout, Bolsonaro ban) cite Wikipedia. The numbers check out, but PKW and the TSE ruling are primary and would sit better against the source hierarchy.
The TBI series' 1990 value of 4 is inferred from the source's "roughly fivefold increase 1990–2019" (19/5 ≈ 4) rather than a published count; consider labelling it as approximate.
why_now: "Europe's longest-running illiberal-populist government" is contestable — Erdoğan has governed Turkey since 2003. "The EU's longest-running" would be unambiguous.
institute.global returned HTTP 429 to both curl and WebFetch (rate limiting/bot protection, not a dead link — the page is indexed and live). Worth one manual click before publish.
verdicts.post_run_fixes_applied: All 3 blocking issues fixed per the critic's prescribed corrections before persisting (2026-08-11): Guardrail V-Dem scoping, PopuList series points, Erosion Diagnostician citation.

notes: The lead's three poles (disease / immune response / misdiagnosis) map cleanly to Erosion Diagnostician, Corrective Populist, and Measurement Skeptic, but Guardrail Institutionalist and National Conservative only find their seats via the subtitle's four-locus enumeration ('unchecked executives of any stripe', 'technocratic closure'). That works — the subtitle does the disambiguating — but readers who stop at the lead may collapse Guardrail into the disease camp and NatCon into immune-response. A lead phrasing that hints the 'disease' pole itself splits (populists vs. executives generally) would be sharper, though not required.

National Conservative and Corrective Populist share the 'technocratic closure' locus in the subtitle despite diagnosing it very differently (legitimate reclamation vs. left-populist re-politicization). Both can locate themselves there, so this is not blocking, but 'the technocratic closure that provoked the revolt' reads slightly more in Mouffe's register than Hazony's; a phrase like 'in institutions that stopped answering to voters' would carry both camps equally.

The values paragraph's central clash (majority overriding courts = demos heard vs. democracy stops being liberal) is a genuine two-sided value axis, and the Measurement Skeptic is correctly routed to the empirical branch rather than forced into it. Good structure: the empirical/values split does real narrowing work and stakes checkable predictions (incumbent behavior rates, behavioural-vs-expert index divergence, Poland's restoration record) without a house verdict.
'Nobody in this fight rejects elections' is an effective shared-ground opener and is accurate for all five camps as drafted.

Q4 (T1, above fold) uses the term 'concept stretching' in the question text without any compact-layer gloss; the 'why' explains the coder-mood half but not the stretching half. A smart general reader can roughly infer it, and the detail defines it properly, so this is polish not blocking. If touched, a two-word gloss in the why (e.g. 'or a shift in coder mood and ever-looser definitions') would close it.

Basics stat 2 ('Countries autocratizing vs. democratizing'): the headline value '44 countries' covers only the autocratizing side of a 'vs.' label. Mitigated because the ranked series (44 vs 18, with population shares) renders above the fold and the note states the 2:1 comparison, so the reader does see both sides; noting for pattern-awareness only.

All four above-fold basics stats point in the 'decline is real' direction; the Measurement Skeptic has no supporting stat anywhere in basics. The above-fold picture stays correct because Q4 and the Measurement Skeptic steelman ('the hard indicators barely moved') are both T1 and visible, so the contest over the numbers is above the fold even if no counter-stat is. Acceptable as-is.

Crux subtitle names four damage-locations (populists attacking courts / unchecked executives / technocratic closure / the measuring instruments) for five positions; the National Conservative reading (what's called backsliding is majorities legitimately reclaiming overreaching institutions) is only loosely folded into 'technocratic closure that provoked the revolt.' Defensible compression, but if the subtitle is ever revised, a fifth clause would make the position count match.

Below-fold only (T2, so not blocking on my dimension): the 'Populist leaders in power' note says the count 'fell by more than a third by early 2024' while the caveat that this predates Trump's return and 2024-25 elections lives only in the detail; a normal-reveal reader could take away a declining trend the source itself does not claim. Worth a clause in the note if that stat is ever promoted to T1.

Stat 4 (trust) makes no trend claim in the compact layer, so the like-for-like comparability caveat living only in the detail is fine; the note correctly states both the 39% and 44% shares with their denominator (30 OECD countries, 2023).

Q4 question text uses 'concept stretching' in the compact layer without a gloss in its why line (the why covers coder bias only); the term is near-self-explanatory and is properly defined at first use in the Measurement Skeptic detail (Sartori), so it clears the parity bar, but adding two words of gloss to the why would remove the wobble.

'Militant-democracy' appears in two compact slots (Bolsonaro stat label, T2 tolerance question). Both are glossed by adjacent compact text, but the Bolsonaro label's ' · a militant-democracy case' tag is the least-supported instance since the gloss only arrives in the note; consider ' · when courts ban candidates' if a plainer tag is wanted.

National Conservative detail: the Le Pen sentence runs ~110 words across six stacked clauses (conviction → appeal → sentence arithmetic → backdating → 2027 eligibility → her declaration). Register-appropriate content, but one sentence break would bring it to parity with the other position details.
'V-Dem' appears as a bare name in four compact stat labels; acceptable as source attribution (the first T1 detail explains its expert-coder methodology), just noting the density.

All detail fields genuinely add over their compact lines (mechanism, precise figures, methodology caveats, defined terms of art); no restatement cases found. Compact notes consistently round numbers to retainable forms.

Basics fold is coherent: the four T1 stats give scale (74% under autocracy), direction (44 vs 18 countries), the electoral phenomenon (23% far-right share), and the mechanism dispute (39% trust). The T1/T2 boundary is a genuine drop-off: Freedom House's 20-year streak corroborates the V-Dem stats already above the fold rather than adding a new axis, and its demotion avoids double-counting the decline narrative.

'Populist leaders in power 1990–2024' (T2) is arguably the most literally on-topic stat for the populism half, and a case exists for swapping it with 'Trust in national government' (T1). But the demotion is defensible on presentation grounds: its own detail concedes the early-2024 count is stale (predates Trump's return), which weakens it as a headline number, while trust directly powers the symptom-vs-cause T1 question. Judgment call, not a defect.

The why_now hook (Hungary 2026, 'whether backsliding can be reversed at the ballot box') points at a below-fold question (T2 ballot-box reversal). Mild tension, but not blocking: each of the four above-fold T1 questions anchors one of the five positions' defining disputes, and reversal is a second-order question downstream of the erosion-vs-artifact and playbook questions. Promoting it would force demoting a position-defining dispute, a worse trade.
Questions T2/T3 boundary is right: the cordon-sanitaire question (T3) is a narrower operational sub-case of the militant-democracy question (T2), so the ordering reflects genuine generality drop-off.
Basics T3 items (Poland turnout, Bolsonaro ban) are correctly deepest: both are single-case illustrations serving below-fold questions, exactly what the deep layer is for.
Positions 5/5 above fold with prevalence-first order (85/45/45/40/25) is correct; all five are genuine camps and hiding any would break the honest non-balance rule.

prevalence_basis.name: Erosion Diagnostician
prevalence_basis.sketch: Populist incumbents reliably attack courts, media, and elections; the evidence shows populism driving a global wave of democratic decay.

prevalence_basis.name: Guardrail Institutionalist
prevalence_basis.sketch: The core problem is executive aggrandizement of any stripe; the answer is stronger constitutional design, courts, and norm enforcement.

prevalence_basis.name: National Conservative
prevalence_basis.sketch: Backsliding talk is a partisan cudgel; elected majorities reclaiming captured institutions from progressive elites is democracy working.

prevalence_basis.name: Corrective Populist
prevalence_basis.sketch: Populism re-politicizes what elites foreclosed and gives voice to the ignored; a democratic populism can renew, not destroy, democracy.

prevalence_basis.name: Technocracy Critic
prevalence_basis.sketch: The disease is depoliticized rule by experts and juristocracy; populism is the symptom, and treating it as the cause misses the point.

prevalence_basis.name: Measurement Skeptic
prevalence_basis.sketch: Objective indicators show far less decline than expert-coded indices; backsliding claims stretch concepts and bake in coder bias.
